key_terms.meaning: Solvent-rich and carrier-rich layers leaving a stage.
K = y<sub>A</sub>/x<sub>A</sub> (mass fractions at the ends of a tie line); on solute-free ratios Y = K′X.
β = (y<sub>A</sub>/y<sub>B</sub>)/(x<sub>A</sub>/x<sub>B</sub>); must be well above 1.

key_terms.term: Binodal curve, tie line, plait point
key_terms.meaning: Boundary of the two-phase region; line joining two layers in equilibrium; point where the layers become identical.
FM/MS = S/F on mixing; E/M = RM/RE on splitting.
ε = K′S/B, solute to extract over solute left, per ideal stage.
X<sub>n</sub> = X<sub>0</sub>/(1 + ε)<sup>n</sup> for equal fresh-solvent portions.
Actual change in a stage over the ideal change; overall efficiency = ideal stages/real stages.
X<sub>N</sub>/X<sub>0</sub> = (ε − 1)/(ε<sup>N+1</sup> − 1) for pure solvent; 1/(N + 1) at ε = 1.
Δ = F − E<sub>1</sub> = R<sub>N</sub> − S; every line R<sub>n</sub>E<sub>n+1</sub> passes through it.
Pinch at the feed end for immiscible liquids: S<sub>min</sub> = B(X<sub>0</sub> − X<sub>N</sub>)/(K′X<sub>0</sub>).
A ≥ Q<sub>c</sub>/u<sub>t</sub>, with Stokes u<sub>t</sub> = Δρgd²/(18μ<sub>c</sub>).
Z = H<sub>OR</sub>N<sub>OR</sub>; N<sub>OR</sub> from x<sub>1</sub>/x<sub>2</sub> and ε.
Inert solid with retained solution L = rI; clear solution V = M − L.
All solute dissolved; retained solution and overflow at the same y.
A·f, stroke times frequency; mean liquid speed 2Af.
ω²r/g times gravity; settling speed rises in the same ratio.
Above 31.0 °C and 73.8 bar; solvent power set by density (pressure).
Stationary beds in series; liquor inlet and outlet advanced one tank per cycle.
V<sub>1</sub> = W + A − L; washing stages 2 to N with E = W/L: y<sub>N</sub>/y<sub>1</sub> = (E − 1)/(E<sup>N</sup> − 1).

takeaways: Extraction pays when distillation is poor; the solvent needs selectivity, a useful K, low mutual solubility with the carrier and easy recovery.
Every stage calculation is a mass balance: on the triangle the lever rule draws it, on solute-free ratios it becomes algebra.
Cross-current stages each remove the fraction ε/(1 + ε) of what is left, so X<sub>n</sub> = X<sub>0</sub>/(1 + ε)<sup>n</sup>, with a limit e<sup>−K′S<sub>T</sub>/B</sup> however many stages.
Counter-current flow gets more recovery from the same solvent because the extract leaves near equilibrium with the richest feed; stages come from the difference point or the Kremser equation.
A contactor must disperse and then separate; settler area follows the continuous-phase flow and the drop settling velocity, column height follows transfer units.
Leaching balances are written on the inert solid; the retained solution L = rI carries most of the lost solute.
In counter-current leaching of a dry feed, stage 1 has a smaller overflow than the washing stages; treat it separately and apply the Kremser equation to stages 2 to N.
Pulsing, centrifuging and supercritical solvents change how fast phases meet and part, or how strong the solvent is; the equilibrium balances do not change.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for stage calculations on solute-free ratios or the triangular diagram, a sketch and description of extraction and leaching equipment, and the counter-current leaching battery including the Shanks system; supercritical and centrifugal extraction usually come as short descriptive questions.

bank.q: Explain the triangular diagram for a type I ternary liquid system: how a composition is read, the binodal curve, tie lines, the plait point and the lever rule. Show how the amounts of extract and raffinate are found for one equilibrium stage.
outline: Binodal curve, one- and two-phase regions
Tie lines and plait point; type I and II
E and R by the lever rule and by balances
answer: Coordinates. In an equilateral triangle each corner is a pure component: solute A at the top, carrier B at the bottom left, solvent S at the bottom right. A point on a side is a binary mixture. For an inside point, the mass fraction of A is its perpendicular distance from side BS divided by the height; likewise for B (from side AS) and S (from side AB). The three fractions add to 1, so in practice they are read off grid lines parallel to the sides. A right-angled version (xA up, xS across) works the same way.

Binodal curve. For a type I system B and S are partly miscible while A mixes with both. The binodal (solubility) curve starts near B on side BS, rises to a maximum and returns near S. Outside it the mixture is one liquid; inside it splits into two layers, one on the raffinate branch near B and one on the extract branch near S.

Tie lines and plait point. A tie line joins two layers in equilibrium; it is measured experimentally and normally slopes because A favours one layer. Tie lines shorten as A increases and vanish at the plait point, where both layers have the same composition. A type II system (two partly miscible pairs, A–S and B–S) has a two-phase band across the diagram and no plait point.
Mixing. When F kg of feed and S kg of solvent are mixed, the mixture point M lies on the straight line FS with FM/MS = S/F; its composition is the weighted average, xA,M = (F xA,F + S yA,S)/(F + S).

Splitting. If M lies inside the binodal curve, the tie line through it (interpolated between measured tie lines) gives the extract E and raffinate R at its ends. The lever rule gives the amounts: E/M = RM/RE and R/M = ME/RE, where the lengths are measured on the tie line.

answer.text: Numbers. 100 kg of 30 % acetic acid in water mixed with 120 kg of solvent: M = 220 kg at xA = 0.136, xS = 0.545. With the tie line R (xA = 0.100, xS = 0.030) to E (yA = 0.1543, yS = 0.800):

answer: Sketch. Draw the triangle with the binodal dome and plait point, two or three sloping tie lines, F on side AB, the line FS, M on it and the tie line through M ending at R and E.
Check. The solvent and water balances close (120.1 kg and 69.9 kg against 120 and 70 kg fed), and 22.7 kg of the 30 kg of acid (75.8 %) is in the extract.

bank.q: List the characteristics of a good solvent for liquid–liquid extraction and explain why each matters.
answer: Selectivity β = (yA/yB)/(xA/xB), the separation factor between solute and carrier. It must be well above 1; at β = 1 the extract has the same solute-to-carrier ratio as the raffinate and no separation results. For the acid–water example in this unit β = 29.4.

Distribution coefficient K = yA/xA. A large K means each kilogram of solvent carries more solute, so the solvent flow, the equipment and the solvent-recovery load are smaller. K need not exceed 1 if the solvent is cheap and easily recovered, but small K means large flows.
Low mutual solubility with the carrier. Solvent dissolved in the raffinate is lost (or must be stripped), and carrier dissolved in the extract dilutes the product and must be separated later.

Recoverability. The solvent is nearly always recovered by distillation from the extract, so its boiling point should be well away from that of the solute, it should form no azeotrope with it, and its latent heat should be low.
Density difference between the saturated layers, so the drops settle quickly in a settler or a column; differences of the order of 100 kg/m³ or more are comfortable.

Interfacial tension in the right range: high enough that drops coalesce and the layers separate cleanly, low enough that the liquids can be dispersed without great power. Very low tension gives emulsions.
Chemical properties: stable, not reacting with the solute or materials of construction, non-corrosive.

Safety and cost: low toxicity, low flammability (a high flash point), low viscosity for easy pumping and fast mass transfer, low freezing point, cheap and available in quantity. In practice no solvent is best on every count, so the choice is a compromise; solvent-selection guides rank candidates on these properties.

bank.q: With sketches, describe the mixer-settler, the spray, packed and mechanically agitated extraction columns, and the pulsed and centrifugal extractors. State how each disperses and separates the phases and where each is used.
outline: Spray and packed columns; wetting; flooding
answer: Two jobs. Every contactor disperses one liquid as drops in the other to make interfacial area, then lets the drops coalesce so the two layers can leave separately. Stage-wise units do the jobs in separate vessels; differential columns do both continuously with counter-current flow.

Mixer-settler. Sketch a stirred tank discharging into a horizontal settler with a light layer, a dispersion band and a heavy layer, each leaving over a weir. The mixer is sized by residence time (0.5 m³ at 12 m³/h gives 2.5 min) and gives a stage efficiency of 0.8 to 1. The settler area is the continuous-phase flow over the drop settling velocity (8 m³/h at 6.62 m/h needs 1.21 m²). Used where many stages, high flows or solids occur, as in copper and uranium extraction; drawbacks are floor space and solvent inventory.
Spray column. An empty tower; the dispersed liquid is sprayed in at one end and rises (or falls) through the continuous liquid. Cheap and hard to foul, but back-mixing limits it to one or two stages.

Packed column. Rings or structured packing re-form the drops and reduce back-mixing. The packing should be wetted by the continuous phase so that the dispersed phase stays as drops. Capacity is limited by flooding; design at 50–70 % of flooding sets the diameter, and Z = HORNOR sets the height (4.16 transfer units × 0.9 m = 3.74 m in this unit's example).

Mechanically agitated columns. The rotating-disc contactor has discs on a central shaft between stator rings; the Scheibel and Oldshue–Rushton columns have impellers between calming or packed zones; the Karr column reciprocates a stack of perforated plates. Agitation makes small drops, so many stages fit in a short column. Used for many-stage duties with clean liquids.

Pulsed column. A sieve-plate or packed column whose liquid contents are pulsed by a piston or air pulser. Pulse intensity A·f (stroke × frequency) controls drop size: too little gives large drops, too much gives emulsions and early flooding. No moving parts inside, so it is used for radioactive liquors in nuclear fuel reprocessing.

Centrifugal extractors. The Podbielniak extractor spins a drum containing a perforated spiral; the heavy liquid is thrown outward and the light liquid driven inward, counter-currently, in seconds. Annular centrifugal contactors mix in the annulus and separate in the rotor. At 3000 rpm and r = 0.2 m the field is 2012 g. Used where contact time must be short (penicillin) or hold-up small.

Selection. Few stages and dirty liquids: mixer-settlers or spray columns. Many stages and clean liquids: agitated or pulsed columns. Short contact, unstable products or small hold-up: centrifugal extractors. Low density difference or emulsifying systems: centrifugal.

bank.q: Describe the equipment for batch and continuous leaching, including percolation tanks, the Shanks system, agitated vessels, thickeners and moving-bed extractors. Explain how each brings solid and solvent into contact.
answer: Mechanism. The solvent enters the solid, dissolves the solute, and the solution diffuses out through the pores and across a liquid film. Small particles shorten the diffusion path but drain badly; coarse particles drain well but leach slowly. The equipment depends mainly on particle size: coarse solids are leached in beds, fine solids in suspension.

Percolation tanks. A tank with a perforated false bottom holds a bed of coarse solid. Solvent is sprayed or flooded on top and percolates down; the liquor is drawn from below. First runnings are strong, later ones weak. Used for coffee, tea, tanning bark, ores in vats.

Shanks system. A battery of percolation tanks connected by pipes. Fresh solvent enters the tank with the most nearly exhausted solid; the liquor flows through the tanks in order of increasing freshness of solid and leaves as strong liquor from the newest tank. When the oldest tank is spent, it is emptied and refilled with fresh solid and becomes the last tank in the liquor path; the inlet and outlet move one tank round the battery each cycle. The solid never moves, but the flow is counter-current.

Agitated vessels. Fine solids are suspended in the solvent in a stirred tank, batch or in series for continuous work, then separated by settling or filtration. The Pachuca tank is a tall cylinder with a conical base, agitated by air rising in a central draft tube, used for fine ore slurries.

Thickeners and CCD. A Dorr thickener is a shallow tank with a slowly rotating rake; clear overflow leaves at the rim, thickened underflow at the centre of the base. Several thickeners in series with solids going one way and wash liquor the other form continuous counter-current decantation, used for alumina, uranium and gold ores. The underflow still holds solution, which the stage calculation tracks.

Moving-bed extractors for seeds and flakes. Bollman: perforated baskets on a vertical chain; on the way down the solid meets half-miscella sprayed co-currently, on the way up fresh solvent counter-currently. Rotocel: a rotating ring of cells passes under a series of solvent sprays and drains, emptying at one point of each turn. Kennedy: paddles push the solid through a row of tubs against the solvent. Screw extractors (the Hildebrandt type) carry the solid up a U-tube against the solvent.

Choice. Coarse, free-draining solids: percolation, Shanks or moving-bed units. Fine solids: agitated vessels with thickeners or filters. Large throughput of oilseed: Rotocel or similar. Ore slurries: Pachuca tanks and CCD trains. In every case the solid leaves wet, so the retained solution sets the final loss.

bank.q: 400 kg of a solution containing 100 kg of solute A in 300 kg of carrier B is extracted in three ideal cross-current stages with 100 kg of pure solvent each. B and S are immiscible and Y = 2.5X on solute-free ratios. Find the raffinate ratio and the extract after each stage, the overall recovery, and compare with a single stage using all 300 kg. What is the best recovery possible with 300 kg in cross-current?
answer: Stage relation. For each ideal stage with pure solvent: B Xn−1 = B Xn + S Yn with Yn = 2.5Xn, so Xn = Xn−1/1.8333.
Recovery. A recovered = 45.5 + 24.8 + 13.5 = 83.8 kg, so 83.8 % (check: 100 − 16.2 = 83.8 kg). The combined extract is 300 kg of solvent with 83.8 kg A, Y = 0.279 on average.
Single stage with 300 kg. ε = 2.5 × 300/300 = 2.5; X1 = 0.3333/3.5 = 0.0952; A left 28.6 kg; recovery 71.4 %. Splitting the solvent into three equal portions raises recovery from 71.4 % to 83.8 %.
Limit. With very many equal portions, Xn/X0 → e−K′ST/B = e−2.5 = 0.0821, so no cross-current arrangement with 300 kg can recover more than 91.8 %.
Check. Each stage removes ε/(1 + ε) = 45.5 % of the A it receives: 100 → 54.5 → 29.8 → 16.2 kg, consistent with the table.

bank.q: 1000 kg/h of a solution of 200 kg/h solute in 800 kg/h carrier is to be extracted counter-currently with pure solvent to recover 90 % of the solute. B and S are immiscible and Y = 1.8X. Find the minimum solvent rate. Using 1.5 times the minimum, find the number of ideal stages by the Kremser equation and check it by stepping stage by stage; find the extract concentration and locate the difference point.
answer: Targets. X0 = 200/800 = 0.250; 90 % recovery leaves 20 kg/h, XN = 0.025.

Minimum solvent. With a straight equilibrium line and pure solvent, the pinch is at the feed end, where the extract would leave in equilibrium with the feed: Y1* = 1.8 × 0.250 = 0.450. Smin = B(X0 − XN)/Y1* = 800 × 0.225/0.450 = 400 kg/h.

answer.text: Stage-by-stage check from the feed end: Y1 = (B/S)(X0 − XN) = 1.333 × 0.225 = 0.300; Xn = Yn/1.8; Yn+1 = 1.333(Xn − 0.025).

answer: Reading the table. After 4 stages X4 = 0.0253, just above 0.025 (recovery 89.95 %), and Y5 = 0.0005 instead of 0: four stages fall just short. The Kremser equation gives 4.01. Either install 5 ideal stages (Kremser: 93.1 % recovery) or keep 4 stages and raise the solvent slightly above 600 kg/h.
Extract. Y1 = 0.300 kg/kg, so E1 is 600 kg/h of solvent with 180 kg/h of solute (780 kg/h, 23.1 mass% solute).

Difference point. Δ = F − E1 = 1000 − 780 = 220 kg/h containing A = 20, B = 800, S = −600 kg/h. On the right-angled diagram Δ is at xS = −600/220 = −2.73, xA = 20/220 = 0.091, to the left of the triangle; all lines RnEn+1, and FE1 and RNS, pass through it.
Check. Overall solute balance: 200 = 180 + 20 kg/h. S/Smin = 1.5 as specified.

bank.q: 200 kg of a feed containing 25 mass% acid A in water B is contacted in one ideal stage with 150 kg of pure solvent S. The tie line through the mixture joins the raffinate (x<sub>A</sub> = 0.080, x<sub>S</sub> = 0.025) to the extract (y<sub>A</sub> = 0.1929, y<sub>S</sub> = 0.750). Find the mixture point, the masses and compositions of E and R, the acid recovered, K and β. Show how the raffinate would be treated in a second cross-current stage with 100 kg of solvent.
answer: Mixture. M = 200 + 150 = 350 kg holding 50 kg A, 150 kg B and 150 kg S: xA,M = 0.1429, xB,M = 0.4286, xS,M = 0.4286. On the diagram M is on line FS with FM/MS = 150/200 = 0.75.
Compositions. Raffinate R: xA = 0.080, xS = 0.025, xB = 0.895. Extract E: yA = 0.1929, yS = 0.750, yB = 0.0571.

Second cross-current stage. R1 (155.1 kg) is mixed with 100 kg of fresh S. M2 = 255.1 kg with 12.4 kg A and 3.9 + 100 = 103.9 kg S: xA = 0.0486, xS = 0.407. M2 lies on line R1S with R1M2/M2S = 100/155.1. The tie line through M2, read from the equilibrium data, gives E2 and R2, and their masses follow from the same two balances.
Sketch. Triangle with binodal, F at 0.25 on side AB, line FS with M, tie line RE through M, then line R1S with M2.

bank.q: 2000 kg/h of flaked seed containing 20 mass% oil is leached counter-currently with 1200 kg/h of pure hexane. Every underflow retains 0.5 kg of solution per kg of oil-free meal. Find the number of ideal stages for at least 95 % recovery, the strong miscella flow and concentration, and the number of real stages at an overall efficiency of 0.7.
outline: Kremser for stages 2 to N with the solute balance
answer: Basis. Inert meal B = 0.80 × 2000 = 1600 kg/h; oil A = 400 kg/h; retained solution L = 0.5 × 1600 = 800 kg/h in every underflow.
Overflow rates. Overall solution balance: V1 = W + A − L = 1200 + 400 − 800 = 800 kg/h of strong miscella. In stages 2 to N the overflow is W = 1200 kg/h, so E = W/L = 1.5.

answer.text: Equations. For the N − 1 washing stages with pure solvent and the overall oil balance:
answer.pre:
y<sub>N</sub>/y<sub>1</sub> = (E − 1)/(E<sup>N</sup> − 1) = 0.5/(1.5<sup>N</sup> − 1)
400 = V<sub>1</sub>y<sub>1</sub> + L y<sub>N</sub> = 800 y<sub>1</sub> + 800 y<sub>N</sub>

answer: Ideal stages. Five stages give 93.0 %, six give 95.4 %, so 6 ideal stages are needed.
Miscella. With N = 6: V1 = 800 kg/h at y1 = 0.477, carrying 381.6 kg/h of oil; the spent meal carries 800 × 0.0230 = 18.4 kg/h. Check: 381.6 + 18.4 = 400 kg/h.
Real stages. 6/0.7 = 8.6, so 9 real stages (or extractor cells) are installed.

Check of stage 1. The feed is dry, so stage 1 receives the oil as solid and the overflow from stage 2; its overflow (800 kg/h) is smaller than in the washing stages (1200 kg/h). Using E = 800/800 = 1 for the whole battery would be wrong.

bank.q: A packed extraction column must reduce the solute in an aqueous feed from x<sub>1</sub> to x<sub>2</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>/20 with pure solvent. Pilot data give H<sub>OR</sub> = 1.2 m. Find the packed height for ε = mS/R = 1.25 and for ε = 2.0, and comment. The feed then goes to a mixer-settler for a polishing stage: 30 m³/h total flow, a 1.0 m³ mixer, 10 m³/h continuous phase, 200 µm drops, Δρ = 120 kg/m³, μ<sub>c</sub> = 0.8 mPa·s. Find the mixer time and the settler area.
answer: Transfer units. For dilute solutions, a straight equilibrium line and pure solvent: NOR = ln[(x1/x2)(1 − 1/ε) + 1/ε]/(1 − 1/ε), and Z = HORNOR.

Comment. Raising the solvent by 60 % (ε 1.25 → 2.0) cuts the height by 40 %. At ε = 1 the formula becomes NOR = x1/x2 − 1 = 19, so low solvent rates make the column very tall. The optimum balances column cost against the cost of recovering more solvent.
Mixer. t = V/Q = 1.0/30 h = 2.0 min.
Settler. A = Qc/ut = 10/11.8 = 0.85 m² minimum; a real settler is made larger to hold the dispersion band.
Check. Units: (m³/h)/(m/h) = m². Doubling the drop size would quarter the area, which is why the mixer must not be over-stirred into fine drops.

bank.q: A feed of 600 kg/h carrier with 150 kg/h solute (Y = 2.0X, immiscible liquids) can be extracted with 450 kg/h of pure solvent in three ideal stages, either cross-current (150 kg/h to each stage) or counter-current. Compare the recovery, the extract concentration and the solvent each needs for the same recovery, and explain the difference.
answer: Basis. B = 600 kg/h, X0 = 0.25.
Cross-current. ε per stage = 2 × 150/600 = 0.5. X3 = 0.25/1.5³ = 0.0741; solute left 44.4 kg/h; recovery 70.4 %. The combined extract is 450 kg/h of solvent with 105.6 kg/h, an average Y of 0.235.

Solvent to match 87.7 % by cross-current. Need (1 + ε)³ = 0.25/0.0308 = 8.125, so 1 + ε = 2.010, ε = 1.010 per stage, S = 1.010 × 600/2 = 303 kg/h per stage: 909 kg/h in all, twice the counter-current solvent, and the extract would be correspondingly weaker.
Minimum for counter-current. Smin = 600 × (0.25 − 0.0308)/(2 × 0.25) = 263 kg/h; the 450 kg/h used is 1.71 Smin.

Why. In counter-current flow the extract leaves stage 1 in contact with the fresh feed, so it can approach equilibrium with the richest liquid (Y1* = 0.50); the solvent is used to carry solute from every stage. In cross-current flow each solvent portion leaves in equilibrium with a progressively leaner raffinate, so the later portions carry little. It is not that every counter-current stage has a larger driving force; stage 1 meets partly loaded solvent.

Verdict. For continuous plants counter-current is chosen: higher recovery and a stronger extract from the same solvent, so less solvent to recover. Cross-current suits small batches or where the extracts are wanted separately.

bank.q: Evaluate hexane leaching against supercritical CO<sub>2</sub> extraction for 1000 kg of oilseed (20 % oil). For hexane take four ideal counter-current stages, 600 kg of hexane and 0.5 kg of retained solution per kg of meal. For CO<sub>2</sub> take a leaving-fluid loading of 1.0 mass% oil and a CO<sub>2</sub> flow of 2000 kg/h. Compare recovery, solvent use, product quality, safety and cost.
outline: Recovery and solvent per kg oil
answer: Hexane basis. Meal B = 800 kg, oil A = 200 kg, L = 400 kg. V1 = 600 + 200 − 400 = 400 kg; washing factor E = 600/400 = 1.5.

Hexane result. y4/y1 = 0.5/(1.5⁴ − 1) = 0.5/4.0625 = 0.1231. 200 = 400y1 + 400 × 0.1231y1, y1 = 0.445, y4 = 0.0548. Oil lost 400 × 0.0548 = 21.9 kg; recovery 89.0 %. The miscella (400 kg, 44.5 % oil) is distilled and the wet meal is desolventised with steam.

CO2 requirement. 200 kg of oil at 1.0 % in the leaving fluid needs 200/0.010 = 20 000 kg of fluid, i.e. 19 800 kg of CO2, 99 kg per kg of oil, about 9.9 h at 2000 kg/h. This is a minimum: towards the end the fluid leaves unsaturated, so real runs use more.

Recovery. CO2 can approach complete removal because it has no retained-solution loss at the end (the CO2 simply vents from the meal), while the hexane battery loses the oil in the 400 kg of retained solution; more stages would raise hexane recovery (95 % needs more stages, as in the battery questions of this bank).

Quality. CO2 leaves no solvent residue and works at 40–60 °C, which suits flavours, spices and nutraceuticals; hexane products need desolventising and carry trace-residue limits. CO2 is selective (low-polarity components), which can be good or bad depending on the product.

Safety and energy. Hexane is flammable and its vapour must be contained; CO2 is non-flammable and non-toxic but needs vessels at 200–300 bar and energy to recompress about 100 kg of CO2 per kg of oil.

Cost. For bulk edible oil at hundreds of tonnes per day, hexane leaching in moving-bed extractors is far cheaper per tonne. For small, high-value products (hops, spice oleoresins, decaffeination) the CO2 process wins on quality and regulation.
Verdict. Hexane for bulk oilseed; supercritical CO2 for high-value, heat-sensitive or residue-free products.

bank.q: A three-tank Shanks battery treats 1000 kg/h of solid (25 % soluble, 75 % inert) with 600 kg/h of fresh water; each charge retains 0.6 kg of solution per kg of inert. Analyse how the recovery and the strength of the product liquor change if (a) the number of tanks is raised to 4 or 5, and (b) the water is raised to 900 kg/h. Recommend an operating point.
answer: Base data. B = 750 kg/h inert, A = 250 kg/h solute, L = 450 kg/h retained solution. Strong liquor V1 = W + A − L; washing factor in tanks 2 to N, E = W/L.

answer.pre:
y<sub>N</sub>/y<sub>1</sub> = (E − 1)/(E<sup>N</sup> − 1)
A = V<sub>1</sub>y<sub>1</sub> + L y<sub>N</sub>   →   y<sub>1</sub> = A/(V<sub>1</sub> + L·y<sub>N</sub>/y<sub>1</sub>)

answer: (a) More tanks at the same water raise recovery (78.5 → 85.2 → 89.6 %) and also make the product slightly stronger (0.491 → 0.560), because the extra washing stages strip the spent solid better while the strong liquor still leaves the freshest tank. The cost is capital and a longer cycle.

(b) More water raises recovery sharply (78.5 → 91.6 % with 3 tanks) because E rises from 1.33 to 2.0, but the product is weaker (0.491 → 0.327) and larger (400 → 700 kg/h). If the solute is recovered by evaporation, the water to evaporate per kg of solute rises from (400 − 196)/196 = 1.04 to (700 − 229)/229 = 2.06 kg.
Trade-off. Tanks cost capital once; extra water costs evaporation energy every hour. A larger battery at low water gives both high recovery and a strong product.

Recommendation. If the target is about 95 %, use 4 tanks with 900 kg/h (95.9 %) when evaporation is cheap, or 8 tanks with 600 kg/h (96.0 %, product at y = 0.600) when evaporation is expensive. Real tanks fall short of ideal, so divide the ideal count by the overall efficiency.

glossary.def: The component transferred from the feed to the solvent (A).
The feed liquid in which the solute is dissolved (B).
The solvent-rich layer leaving a stage.
The carrier-rich layer leaving a stage.
Ratio of solute concentration in extract to that in the raffinate at equilibrium.
Separation factor of solute over carrier between the two layers; must exceed 1.
Boundary between the one-phase and two-phase regions of a ternary diagram.
Line joining the compositions of two liquid layers in equilibrium.
Point on the binodal curve where the two layers become identical.
Graphical mass balance: the amounts of two streams are in inverse ratio to their distances from the mixture point.
ε = K′S/B, the solute capacity of the solvent relative to the carrier for one stage.
Fresh solvent added to every stage, extracts withdrawn separately.
Feed and solvent enter at opposite ends of a cascade and flow in opposite directions.
Fixed net flow Δ = F − E<sub>1</sub> through which all operating lines of a counter-current cascade pass.
Closed-form stage relation for counter-current cascades with constant flows and a straight equilibrium line.
Actual composition change of a real stage divided by that of an ideal stage.
Stirred mixer followed by a gravity settler; one stage per unit.
Column condition in which the dispersed phase can no longer pass counter-currently and is carried out with the continuous phase.
Agitated extraction column with discs on a central shaft between stator rings.
Return of solvent-free extract product to the extract end of a column to purify the extract.
Stroke times frequency of the liquid pulsation in a pulsed column.
Centrifugal extractor with a perforated spiral in a spinning drum, giving counter-current contact in seconds.
Substance above its critical temperature and pressure, with liquid-like density and gas-like transport properties.
Solid–liquid extraction of a soluble component from a solid with a liquid solvent.
Inert solid together with the solution it retains.
